channel.title: Acme: Tech News
channel.description: Articles about software, publishing and the open web.

item.title: Europe proposes a social-media ban for children under 13
item.description: The proposed EU Kids Act would bar children under 13 from social media, put accounts for ages 13 to 15 under parental control and restrict addictive design features. Platforms could face fines of 6% of global sales, while industry critics warn that large-scale age verification could create new privacy and security risks.

item.title: Google ordered to loosen ad-tech ties but spared a breakup
item.description: A federal judge ordered Google to separate use of its publisher ad server from its AdX exchange, open real-time bids to competing ad servers and accept six years of antitrust monitoring. The remedy stops short of the Justice Department's requested divestiture but could give independent publishers more choice in selling ads.

item.title: San Jose residents challenge a new data-center boom
item.description: San Jose expects each proposed data center to produce $3 million to $6 million a year in tax revenue, but neighborhood and environmental groups want fuller accounting of electricity, water, pollution and public benefits. California lawmakers have sent the governor bills on utility costs and resource transparency.

item.title: Wayback Machine explains access blocks and 429 errors
item.description: The Internet Archive says waves of high-volume traffic forced it to tighten Wayback Machine protections, sometimes blocking real people with HTTP 429 errors. The team is refining how it separates abusive bots from ordinary users and asks anyone wrongly blocked to send browser, operating-system and IP details for review.

item.title: Twenty-five years of mass surveillance face a reckoning
item.description: Cindy Cohn and Bruce Schneier argue that surveillance powers expanded after 9/11 have outlived their rationale while technology has made them far more intrusive. Their case connects constitutional rights, concentrated technical power and the need to replace indiscriminate collection with targeted, accountable methods.

item.title: Political spoiler tactics unsettle Telegraph journalists
item.description: Telegraph staff are debating Reform UK's use of friendly exclusives to pre-empt damaging stories after rival reporters request comment. Critics say the maneuver erodes trust and may discourage journalists from giving subjects enough time to respond, making political coverage less accurate and balanced.

item.title: CSS-Tricks falls quiet again with its future unclear
item.description: Declan Chidlow traces another uncertain chapter for CSS-Tricks: after years of ownership changes and a recent revival, the venerable web-development publication has posted nothing since August 31. With no public explanation from DigitalOcean, contributors and readers are again left wondering whether a valuable open-web archive has a future.

item.title: Study finds the public is expanding, not replacing, its idea of news
item.description: A six-country Reuters Institute study finds 49% of people use a traditional definition of news, while 26% add subjects and formats such as creators, podcasts and short video without abandoning the core. Across groups, verified facts remain foundational; traditional news brands are more likely to be recognized as news and trusted.
item.source: Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism

item.title: Supreme Court rejects mail-ballot limits before the midterms
item.description: The Supreme Court rejected the administration's bid to impose new mail-ballot rules with voting already underway. States may keep their established processes, which account for nearly a third of ballots cast. The majority said the restrictions were likely to fail in court; Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented.

item.title: Georgia voting-system flaw could expose secret ballots
item.description: Researchers say a known flaw can restore Georgia's electronic ballot records to casting order and, when combined with public records, match some voters to their choices. The weakness cannot alter votes, but advocates say it threatens ballot secrecy before November; other states using the equipment have installed a software fix.

item.title: Open-source activity data is less complete than it looks
item.description: Sophia Vargas and Andrew Nesbitt warn that public repositories do not automatically yield trustworthy ecosystem metrics. GHarchive may now capture as little as 20% of some GitHub event types, while APIs omit activity and identifiers vary across sources. Their practical advice: combine datasets, document gaps and handle contributor information responsibly.

item.title: SPJ updates its Code of Ethics for the first time in 12 years
item.description: The Society of Professional Journalists revised its Code of Ethics to reflect fast-changing technology and the growth of independent reporters outside traditional newsrooms. A new line stresses that speed, technology or medium never excuse inaccuracy or unfairness, broadening an old professional standard for today's publishing landscape.

item.title: McClatchy cuts more than 90 union newsroom jobs across 17 papers
item.description: McClatchy is eliminating more than 90 unionized journalism and media jobs across 17 newspapers, about 30% of its union workforce. The Miami Herald loses 32 positions, including El Nuevo Herald's entire writing staff, while local government and investigative beats are also being cut.

item.title: WordPress 7.1 arrives as developers look ahead to 7.2
item.description: WordPress 7.1 is out, alongside Gutenberg 23.8 and 23.9, while the 7.2 cycle targets beta in late October and a December release. September's developer roundup also covers runnable Code Reference examples powered by Playground, declarable keyboard shortcuts, a more extensible Site Editor and continued removal of private DataViews interfaces.

item.title: FOIAball tests a different model for a one-person sports newsroom
item.description: David Covucci's FOIAball newsletter uses public-records requests to break college-football stories for about 7,500 subscribers, 420 of them paid. The one-person publication experiments with subscriptions and institutional support while confronting a familiar problem: strict paywalls can hide the reporting most likely to persuade new readers to subscribe.
